From the error message, however, I would first suggest you check the number of dimensions (scalars, vectors, 2D arrays, 3D arrays, etc) as they appear for variables in your model code.  For example, having both of:

a[i]
and
a[i, j]

in your model code (or in a distribution) would probably give an error like that one.

messages.subject: Re: Define Likelihood as t-distrbution
parts:
As Daniel asked, an example. This one is from https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/linpred.html:  

code <- nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  beta2 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)        # prior for variance components based on Gelman (2006)
  for(i in 1:n) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], sd = sigma) # manual entry of linear predictors
  }
})

But then, instead of y[i] having a dnorm, that y[i] has a dt, with a mean and a sigma/tau
I read in Gelmans's BDA that you can interpret the t distribution as a mixture of normals. I am going to try that now, but it seems so indirect.

How would you specify y[i] as having a t-distribution?

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Define Likelihood as t-distrbution
parts: I would do something like this:

code <- nimbleCode({
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    beta2 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)        # prior for variance components based on Gelman (2006)
    for(i in 1:n) {

##y[i] ~ dnorm(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], sd = sigma) # manual entry of linear predictors
        y[i] ~ dt(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], sigma, df = 3) # manual entry of linear predictors
    }
})

Note that the canonical parameterization (default parameter ordering) for the t-distribution is (mu, sigma, df), so the first argument to dt() will be the mean, the second will be sigma (standard deviation), and the third will be the degrees of freedom (df).

In my example above I hard-coded degrees of freedom as df = 3.  You could also provide a fixed value of df via the constants list, or via the initial values list if you might want to change it, or letting df itself be a model parameter and thus assigning an appropriate prior distribution to the df parameter.

Hope this helps,
Daniel
